sentences.text: Welcome to the black holes tour.
Our starting point is a classic: Cygnus X-1.
This X-ray source, discovered with a rocket in 1964, became the first object identified as a black hole in 1971.
It is 21 solar masses, and once every five and a half days it orbits their common center of mass together with its blue supergiant companion HDE 226868.
Gas drawn from its companion heats to millions of degrees in a bright disk.
Stephen Hawking had bet that this object was not a black hole; in 1990 he conceded his defeat.
Gaia BH1, the closest known black hole to us: 1,560 light-years.
It has neither a disk nor does it emit X-rays; it is completely silent.
Its existence was understood only from a Sun-like star wobbling around an invisible companion once every 186 days.
This wobble was revealed in 2022 by the precise position measurements of the Gaia satellite. It is 9. 6 solar masses, and the diameter of its event horizon is only 56 kilometers.
Here you can see it only by the gravitational lensing that bends the stars in the background.
Our last stop, the first black hole to be photographed: M87 star.
It sits at the center of the giant elliptical galaxy Virgo A, 55 million light-years away.
It is six and a half billion solar masses; its event horizon is six times wider than Pluto's orbit.
The famous orange ring image published in 2019 is the light of the hot gas surrounding its shadow.
From here a jet shoots out at nearly the speed of light and extends for 5,000 light-years.
Our black holes tour has come to an end.
Now we're going to the heart of our galaxy, 26,000 light-years away.
Sagittarius A star, the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way: 4. 3 million solar masses.
The stars around it allowed us to measure its mass; the star named S2 approaches it so closely once every 16 years that it reaches 3 percent of the speed of light.
These observations brought the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2020.
In 2022 the Event Horizon Telescope imaged its shadow.
Right now it is quite quiet; it is swallowing almost no matter.
V404 Cygni, an X-ray nova.
It is silent most of the time, but when gas accumulated from its companion crosses a threshold, it erupts within a few days and becomes the brightest X-ray source in the sky.
These outbursts were observed in 1938, 1956, 1989, and 2015.
During the 2015 outburst, its jets were seen to change direction within seconds; the black hole's spin was dragging spacetime and wobbling the disk like a spinning top.
It is 9 solar masses, and it is the first black hole whose distance was measured directly by radio parallax.
